apx-pack: Backs slide 6, which says the lender view is part of this round’s build. The page shows what that view is for: five decisions a lender makes on a funded project, what each is made on today and what IRIS adds. Funds left to finish: lenders call this keeping the loan in balance, cost to complete against undrawn funds and equity. The QS assesses cost to complete on the footing that the original builder finishes for the contract price (AIQS guidance note, 2019); IRIS adds the builder’s own forecast and what is moving it, such as variations not yet priced, delays not yet notified and trades let against allowances. Completion date: presale settlements repay the loan, and completion past a sunset date lets purchasers rescind. Notices matter because entitlement to time and money depends on notices given in time; a missed notice turns a recoverable delay into the builder’s own cost. Builder failure: what the lender recovers is roughly the completed value, less the cost to finish and the cost of delay; the assessment service is on A9. Scope: IRIS reads the funded project and makes no solvency call on the builder as a company. A builder short of cash tends to show it on the project first, as trades paid late or packages left unlet. Status: planned capability. The design-partner lender decides what the view shows and how it is laid out; the milestone is IRIS for Lenders on a live facility beside the lender’s QS at month 9 (slide 13). Each line on the view links to the source records behind it, and a pack can be exported at each drawdown to sit beside the QS report.
apx-mechanism: Backs slide 4, which shows three lines of the lender’s QS report and what sits beneath each. This page gives all six causes, grouped under the same three lines. The report: a lender’s QS progress drawdown report typically carries a development cost table, work in place valued against the builder’s claim, programme and extensions of time, cost to complete, variations as submitted, approvals, insurances, the builder’s statutory declaration that subcontractors are paid, risk items and a cash flow forecast. The AIQS guidance note (Construction Financing Reports, 2nd edition, 2019) has the QS assess cost to complete on the footing that the original contractor completes the works. Reports commonly state that information supplied was not independently verified. The six causes. 1. Time bars: delay notices, variations, latent conditions and provisional-sum adjustments each carry a notice period; what is near or past its bar decides whether a cost is recoverable or the builder’s own, with liquidated damages on top. 2. Completion: labour on site against the programme, and open defects and rework against practical completion, show whether the date will be reached. 3. Cost not yet notified: the records show delays and changes coming before a notice is lodged, and each carries consequential cost, most visibly preliminaries that extend with the delay. 4. Soft forecast: much of a forecast final cost sits as contingency inside trade budgets and as allowances; how much is still soft is a risk measure in itself. 5. Trades still to let: rates fixed at tender are open to the market once labour and material prices move; scope still to let, or let against an allowance, is price risk still open. 6. Trades paid: with each claim the builder declares that its subcontractors have been paid what is owed (in Queensland, a supporting statement under section 75 of the BIF Act); the payment records show each trade’s claims, approvals and payments. ASIC found false declarations may signal cash flow problems (16-325MR, 2016). Basis: the report column from the AIQS guidance; the causes from the founders’ work inside builders.
apx-since-2021: Backs slide 4’s closing line: since 2021, fixed prices, thinner builders and a trend of in-house delivery have moved more of the risk inside the project. Fixed prices: Probuild, Condev, PBS, Porter Davis, St Hilliers and Roberts Co failed between 2022 and 2025 (reported; the timeline is on slide 3). Thinner builders: construction was 26.1% of companies entering external administration in FY2022, 27.9% in FY2023, 26.9% in FY2024, 24.4% in FY2025 and 24.5% in FY2025-26 (ASIC series 1, 14 September 2026). In-house delivery: where builder and developer are related entities or co-investors, the builder’s margin and the developer’s equity are the same group capital, so a project loss has no second balance sheet to land on and the builder tends to fail with the developer. Bathla’s in-house builder entered administration with the group on 25 August 2026. The share of jobs delivered in-house or by joint venture is a founder observation and has not been measured. Under the builder’s side deed a lender can take the developer’s place if the developer defaults; where the builder has failed too, lenders appoint receivers and fund a replacement builder. Presales: Stamford Capital’s Real Estate Debt Capital Markets Survey, run in March and April 2026, found 37% of construction lenders requiring no presales, up from 29% in 2025 and 18% in 2023, while the share requiring 60 to 100% presales fell from about 45% in 2021 to 8%. Lending has tightened since August 2026 (slide 8). Many jobs still run at arm’s length on a fixed price; the four changes are observed developments, with sources on A7.
apx-reach: Backs slide 10, which shows the chain of documents: drawdown condition, tender condition, head contract clause, side deed. Row 1: the lender’s QS report is required by the facility and paid for by the borrower, so a lender-required, borrower-paid report on the project is established practice. A payment-control vendor has also said that some lenders make its product a condition of lending on certain jobs (vendor claim, November 2025). Row 2: the facility agreement binds the borrower. The builder is bound by what it signs: the tender and award conditions, the head contract, and the builder’s side deed (also called a tripartite deed), signed by lender, developer and builder at financial close, which lenders already require. An IRIS clause sits there: read-only API access to that project’s systems, for monitoring, for that project. Row 3: a builder on a job under way owes nothing new, so the first conditions go on new facilities, extensions and refinances, when the loan is re-papered. Row 4: reasons to refuse are removed up front. Nothing is written back, the builder sees findings before the lender, the view covers the funded project and nothing beyond it, and the lender sees whether the job is forecast to lose money and by how much, while rates and subcontract prices stay with the builder. That a refusal reads as a signal to the lender is a hypothesis until a lender adopts. Row 5: the builder’s duty stands on its own and is not a precondition to its payment claims, because a contractual precondition to payment claims was held void in BRB Modular v AWX [2015] QSC 218. The drawdown condition is met by an exported pack, so a builder cannot hold up the developer’s drawdown. Subcontract confidentiality terms decide what trade data can be shown. Each lender adopts the condition on its own terms. To be confirmed with lawyers at the month-9 legal opinion; not legal advice.
apx-sizing: Backs the market tiles on slide 11. Each step is a line on the Market sheet of the workbook, and each input is on the Inputs sheet with its source and type. Measured or reported: the IBISWorld segment revenues (E3019: medium-rise $18.9bn plus high-rise $14.6bn; E3021, commercial and industrial building: $70.9bn), the major-market shares (developers and REITs fund 88% of multi-unit and 73% of commercial work) and the state shares (Queensland 19.6% of multi-unit work done and 18.2% of commercial establishments); the ABS apartment completion time of 29 months. Estimates: the 65% share of commercial work on jobs of $10M or more, the 24-month commercial build period, and the debt stack at about 1.2 times the build contract. The average facility is $80M at the owner's direction (D-50, 26 November 2026), so the average contract is $66.7M: IRIS targets the upper end of the market, mid- and high-rise jobs carrying senior and mezzanine debt. Cross-checks on job size, all below $66.7M: the top 50 builders started 722 projects worth $43.9bn in 2025, about $61M each (Hubexo); Brisbane and Gold Coast apartment projects on hold average about $48M (PRD, September 2026); a listed lender’s senior construction loans average about $39M (June 2026). Revenue potential: 2,080 developer-funded jobs at $120,000 (15 bps on $80M, at the $10,000 a month cap), 520 other jobs at $42,000, plus assessments at 4% of funded jobs a year at $35,000. A larger average job means fewer jobs, so the total moves little with job size. Queensland: 390 facilities and 100 builder jobs; South East Queensland is about 79% of the state’s building pipeline (CSQ, 2026). Out of scope: low-rise apartments, townhouses and house building, which are mostly jobs under $10M, and public work, which carries no construction facility. Not counted: insurers and surety providers, who hold about $8.7bn of security on these jobs.
apx-model: Backs the base case on slide 11. The workbook runs five years in three cases, with inputs on one sheet and formulas elsewhere. Lender line: lenders adopt at months 12, 18, 22, 26, 29, 32, 34 and 36, then roughly six a year to 20 at month 60. The cadence is a company target. Each lender with the condition adds 0.8 new facilities a month, plus ten re-papered from its existing book over 18 months at extensions and refinances; facilities leave after a 24-month term. The fee is 15 bps a year on the facility limit, with a floor of $3,500 and a cap of $10,000 a month. The average facility is the average build contract times the debt multiple, so this page and A5 price the same facility (D-49): $66.7M at 1.2 times in the base case ($80M), $85M at 1.2 times in the upside ($102M, with a $12,500 cap) and $40M at 1.2 times in the conservative case ($48M, at 12.5 bps) (D-50, 26 November 2026). The base facility pays the cap, $120,000 a year. Builder line: R&D deployments are unpaid until IRIS reconciles to the builder’s own cost reports; two pilots pay from month 6, then a new builder joins at intervals of four to eight months, each starting with two jobs and growing to six. Years 2 and 4: 3 and 14 lenders on 30 and 229 facilities; 22 and 58 paid builder jobs; 18 and 69 people. Assessments: from month 30, at $35,000, benchmarked to QS report fees. People: founders from month 1 at $100K plus 12% superannuation, then $180K from Year 3; hires start after the seed; analysts one per eight live jobs, a lender success manager per two lenders, two engineers plus one per 1.5 lenders. Other costs: Year 1 matches the use of funds on slide 13; cloud and model costs are $250 a month per live job; 8% commission on new facility fees; $4,000 to connect each facility; contingency is 5% of costs from Year 2. Funding: a $3M seed at month 15 in all cases; a Series A is optional and shown separately. Sensitivities, base case: the base facility sits at the cap, so a larger facility or a higher fee adds nothing until the cap moves; each $10M of average facility below $80M takes about $4.6M off Year 5 revenue, and each basis point of fee below 15 is about $2.5M in Year 5. Each mature lender is about $2.2M a year of fees (about 19 facilities); each paid builder job is $42K a year. Results: revenue $0.19M / $2.3M / $9.3M / $22.7M / $40.5M; EBITDA −$0.48M / −$0.31M / $2.4M / $8.9M / $18.1M. Upside $77M and conservative $6.2M in Year 5.

apx-landscape: Backs slide 9. About sixty products and firms were reviewed in October 2026 across eight categories, with four Australian entrants added on 4 November (Korrix, Cintech, Vyne and SteelCap, which is a landing page) and the lender-side and Australian builder-side sites re-read on 26 November 2026: builder project-management platforms (Procore, Oracle Aconex, Autodesk Construction Cloud, Trimble Viewpoint, CMiC, Buildertrend, Fieldwire); builder ERP and cost systems (Jobpac, Cheops, Workbench, Premier, Buildxact, Simpro, Lentune); trade payment and compliance (Payapps, IPEX, Earlytrade, Textura, GCPay, Queensland project trust accounts); lender-side draw and monitoring tools (Built, Rabbet, Land Gorilla, Northspyre, nCino, Abrigo); owner project controls (Mastt, Kahua, InEight, Primavera, Asite, Aphex); AI on construction records (Datagrid, Document Crunch, Trunk Tools, Alloovium, Octant, Slate, nPlan, Buildots, Doxel, OpenSpace, ALICE, Briq); credit and counterparty data (CreditorWatch, Equifax iCIRT, illion, Dun and Bradstreet); and the service incumbents (the lender’s QS firms; KordaMentha, McGrathNicol, FTI, Deloitte, KPMG). Three questions were asked of each: does it reconcile across source systems; does it give the lender a project-level position; is it written into facility documents. The lender’s QS report meets the third as established practice; IPEX’s vendor claims the third for some lenders; Built, Rabbet and Land Gorilla are required operationally by US lenders, with no facility wording found, and Built reads Procore financials at the head-contract draw level. Cross-system reconciliation exists builder-side (Datagrid, Slate, Trunk Tools, Alloovium, Briq) and lender-side on submitted packages (Built); none found combines both and reports outward to builder, developer and lender. Limits: public sources; in-house tools at Tier 1 builders or lenders cannot be seen; IPEX’s own site was not readable in the review session, so its material is as reported in sponsored articles. We would consider a partnership with a product close enough in logic to merge with. The dated sources are in the repository’s research register.
apx-recovery: Backs the references to distressed-project assessments on slides 2, 3, 6, 10 and 11. Proposed and not yet demonstrated: the platform is proven on builder pilots and shaped with a lender design partner first; assessments are offered as part of scaling, at a separate fee per engagement, because distress is where the information problem is most expensive and where a lender already pays outside advisers. The first assessment is a controlled one on a historic record set, scored against the outcome reached, before any live engagement. Fee: fixed per engagement and no share of the recovery, so IRIS has no stake in what it reports; $35,000 in the model, benchmarked to QS report fees; about 14 engagements in Year 5, about 2% of revenue. What it gives: where the project stands across the delivery domains, each finding valued, dated and linked to its record, and a register of gaps. An incoming builder will not take liability for the failed builder’s work, so it prices what it cannot see; a position traced to the records, with gaps listed, narrows what it has to price blind. Speed: a first position in days from access is the design aim; it depends on how complete the records are. Access: before an appointment, the facility’s information rights and the builder’s side deed; after one, a receiver appointed over the developer takes the developer’s rights under the head contract and can give consent, and if the builder is in administration its administrator controls its books and software subscriptions, so access needs the administrator’s agreement. The strongest case is IRIS on the project before a failure. What stays with others: the QS, the valuer and the insolvency practitioner; IRIS does not advise on the decision, value the asset, certify cost to complete or assess the builder’s solvency. The legal pathway is confirmed with lawyers at the month-9 opinion; not legal advice.
apx-risks: Backs the milestones on slide 13. Six risks, each with the action and the point at which we will know. The first two are the ones the round is built to answer: lender adoption is unproven, and builder access rests so far on one R&D partnership. Lender: a design-partner lender is engaged in months 1 to 3 and shapes the view; IRIS runs on a live facility beside its QS at month 9; the first drawdown condition at month 12 is a company target, and the seed at months 15 to 18 is raised on a product in paid use with or without it. Builders: the builder gets IRIS’s view of its own job first, nothing is written back and rates stay with it. Connections: builder-authorised API connections, one adapter per system, built system by system, with a register per project of what it runs; Procore first. Reliance: IRIS is reconciled to builders’ own cost reports and to three historic record sets before a lender relies on it; professional indemnity cover is sized for lender use and reliance terms are set with the design partner; IRIS certifies nothing, and no accuracy figure or security certification is claimed today. Competition: platforms report to their own customer, and requiring one would dictate the builder’s software; QS and restructuring firms could add the capability and are as likely to be channels as rivals; Procore with Datagrid is the platform to watch (slide 9). Sales cycles: lender procurement, panels and legal review are slow; if the first facility slips to month 18 the seed is needed by month 15. Two further risks sit with assessments on A9: access after an appointment, and pricing, which is a fixed fee so that IRIS has no stake in the recovery it reports on.
